cases.label: Case 1
cases.title: Smoke and scent
cases.question: Where did frankincense and myrrh come from, and why would anyone cross a desert for them?

cases.label: Case 2
cases.title: Spices across water
cases.question: How did pepper from India reach a Roman soldier near Hadrian's Wall?

cases.label: Case 3
cases.title: Connection, conflict, crusade
cases.question: How did trade carry beliefs, words and ideas as well as goods?

cases.label: Case 4
cases.title: World in motion
cases.question: Why did Europeans risk everything to find a new route to the Spice Islands?

cases.label: Case 5
cases.title: Conquest and control
cases.question: Why would anyone burn the trees that made them rich?

cases.label: Epilogue
cases.title: From empire to masala
cases.question: If spices are everywhere now, what happened to the mystery?

steps.title: The invisible trade
body: For thousands of years, spices moved across deserts and oceans. Yet today the trade is surprisingly hard to see. Spices were eaten, burned or used up, and the objects scattered.
The gold pins mark places Marc and Marina have visited. The dashed pins are places they still hope to reach.

steps.title: Kochi: the smell of pepper
body: Marina first met the spice trade here, in Kochi on India's Malabar coast, where sacks of black pepper filled warehouses in the narrow streets.
The word spice shares a root with species and special: something particular, from far away.

steps.title: Where the resins grow
body: Frankincense and myrrh are dried tree sap. The trees grow only in a few harsh, dry places: southern Arabia, the island of Socotra and the Horn of Africa.
Click the dots to name each source.

steps.title: Still for sale in Venice
body: In Venice, thousands of kilometres from those trees, Marc and Marina found a shop selling dozens of resins under glass. The labels name Socotra and Yemen.
Open the photos. What can they prove, and what can't they?

steps.title: The land no one has found
body: Around 1470 BCE, Queen Hatshepsut of Egypt sent five ships to a land called Punt. They came back with frankincense trees.
No one knows where Punt was. That's why the map shows a cloud, not a pin.

steps.title: Legends as marketing
body: The Greek historian Herodotus was told that winged serpents guarded the frankincense trees, and giant birds built nests of cinnamon on cliffs no one could climb.
Stories like these hid the real sources and pushed prices up.

steps.title: The incense road
body: Follow the line north. From about 300 BCE, camel caravans carried incense up the edge of Arabia, stopping at desert wells and towns.

steps.title: Petra
body: The Nabataeans controlled the caravans and grew rich. They carved their capital, Petra, into red cliffs in what is now Jordan.
Their road on to the port of Gaza is lined with forts and towns, now a UNESCO World Heritage site in Israel's Negev.

steps.title: The end of the road, in New York
body: At the Met in New York, the authors found an incense burner made in Damascus in the 1300s, near the north end of these routes.
It is more than 9,000 km from where it was used. Evidence travels.

steps.title: Dots in the sea
body: Far to the east, a few small volcanic islands in today's Indonesia were the world's only source of cloves (the Moluccas) and nutmeg and mace (the Banda Islands).
Island sailors carried them west to Java, Malacca and India. Some crossed the whole ocean and settled Madagascar.

steps.title: Berenike
body: Berenike was a port on Egypt's Red Sea coast. By Roman times, Indian traders lived and worshipped here.
Archaeologists found Indian foods, Sanskrit writing and a jar holding about 7.5 kg of black pepper.

steps.title: Pepper reaches Britain
body: Now follow the pepper: across the desert to the Nile, down to Alexandria, across the sea to Rome, and north to the edge of the empire.
A soldier near Hadrian's Wall wrote about cooking with it.

steps.title: Riding the monsoons
body: The Indian Ocean's winds reverse with the seasons. For half the year they blow toward India; then they blow back toward Africa and Arabia.
Press Play the year on the dial and watch the arrows turn.

steps.title: A captain's guidebook
body: Around 40 CE, a Greek captain wrote the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a list of ports and what you could buy in each.
His route ran down the Red Sea, along Africa and across to India on the monsoon.

steps.title: Khadija's caravans
body: In Mecca, a wealthy merchant named Khadija hired a young man called Muhammad to lead her caravans to Syria. Later they married.
As Islam spread, it travelled with traders who shared a faith, a language and rules for fair dealing.

steps.title: The Swahili coast
body: Along East Africa, a chain of trading cities grew rich on the Indian Ocean trade. Persian and Arab traders settled and married into local families.
Swahili, the coast's language, is Bantu with many Arabic and Persian words.

steps.title: Kilwa
body: Kilwa minted its own coins, built in coral stone, and served food on Chinese porcelain.
It's on the authors' wish list. For now it's a dashed pin: still searching.

steps.title: Córdoba
body: Abd al-Rahman, a prince who escaped a massacre of his family in Syria, reached Spain in 755 and made Córdoba his capital. Muslims, Christians and Jews here shared ideas about food, medicine and science.
One of these photos may not be what its file name says.

steps.title: Pharmacy or spice shop?
body: The Crusades brought war but also exchange. Europe developed a taste for pepper, ginger and cloves.
There was no line between a spice shop and a pharmacy. Look at the jars from Padua and Venice.

steps.title: Venice: built on spice
body: Venice had no farmland. It grew rich on trade, above all in spices, sold at Rialto and carried north by German merchants from their fondaco. The word comes from the Arabic funduq.
Which of these pieces of evidence are still where they were, and which have moved?

steps.title: Follow the pepper
body: Each year Venice's galley convoy, the muda, sailed to Alexandria to meet pepper that had come from India by sea and caravan.
Every stop added taxes and profit. Move the month dial to see when each leg sailed.

steps.title: A web of ports
body: By the 1400s, great ports had grown up where the monsoon routes met.
This is a web: many cities, many middlemen, no single owner.

steps.title: Malacca
body: Malacca sat on the narrow strait every ship between China and India had to pass. Arab, Chinese, Indian and Javanese merchants traded side by side.
A Portuguese visitor wrote that whoever controlled Malacca had his hand on the throat of Venice.

steps.title: Calicut
body: On India's Malabar coast, Calicut was called the City of Spices. Its ruler, the Zamorin, grew rich from pepper.
He kept separate rooms where Muslim, Christian, Hindu and Jewish merchants could each do business.

steps.title: Zheng He's treasure fleet
body: Between 1405 and 1433, China sent seven huge fleets across the Indian Ocean under Admiral Zheng He, a Muslim. They reached Malacca, Calicut, Hormuz and East Africa.
After he died, China stopped the voyages.

steps.title: A king who didn't exist
body: Europeans still didn't know where spices came from. Legends filled the gap, including Prester John, an imaginary Christian king they hoped would help them fight Muslim powers.
Watch his kingdom move: first somewhere in the Indies, later in Ethiopia.

steps.title: Hampi
body: The Venetian traveller Niccolò de' Conti visited this great Hindu capital in the 1400s.
Its kings bought warhorses shipped from Arabia and Persia. Look at the horses carved into the temple bases.

steps.title: A map made of stories
body: Back in Venice around 1450, the monk Fra Mauro turned travellers' stories, including de' Conti's, into a great world map. It showed Africa as a continent you could sail around.
His map hangs in Venice. A copy made for Portugal has been lost. Open it and flip it north-up.

steps.title: The race
body: Portugal and Spain wanted to skip the middlemen. Dias rounded southern Africa in 1488. Columbus sailed west in 1492 and landed in the Bahamas. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.
Magellan's ship circled the globe; it came home in 1522 with 26 tons of cloves.

steps.title: Expulsion
body: In 1492 Spain ordered its Jews to convert or leave. Muslims were later forced to convert too.
Doña Gracia Nasi ran a secret network that moved people along trade routes to safety in the Ottoman Empire.

steps.title: Venice, 1516
body: Some refugees reached Venice. In 1516 the city made Jews live in one walled neighbourhood: the first ghetto.
Its five old synagogues are still there, hidden behind plain outside walls.

steps.title: Cutting out the middlemen
body: The Portuguese came to conquer, not only to buy. They seized Malacca in 1511.
Compare these lines with the web of ports in Case 3: a few direct routes, run by one country or company.

steps.title: The Banda Islands
body: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) wanted total control of nutmeg. In 1621 it conquered the Banda Islands, killing and enslaving most of the people.
Elsewhere it destroyed clove trees it couldn't guard, to keep prices high.

steps.title: Spice runs the other way
body: Chili peppers from the Americas spread fast to Africa, India and China and changed cooking there.
As spices became common, they became cheap. Profits moved to a new crop: sugar. That's the authors' last book.

steps.title: Salt and freedom
body: In 1930, Gandhi marched to the sea at Dandi to make salt, breaking a British law. At Calicut, where da Gama had landed, volunteers scooped salt from the beach.
India became independent in 1947.

steps.title: Masala: mixture
body: Berbere, the spice blend of Ethiopia and Eritrea, uses ingredients from four continents. Follow the lines.
Nutmeg now grows in Grenada and cloves in Zanzibar. Spices are both far and near.

steps.title: Thessaloniki
body: In Thessaloniki, the authors found a shop selling herbs and spices by weight.
Which of these might have travelled the furthest? Can you tell?

steps.title: Where we're going next
body: The case isn't closed. After Dubai, Marc and Marina head to Wadi Dawkah in Oman, where frankincense trees still grow.
The dashed pins mark places where the evidence is still waiting. This map will grow as the book does.

evidence.title: Resins for sale in Venice
evidence.site: Resin shop, San Marco, Venice (shop name to confirm)
evidence.then: Frankincense and myrrh came from trees that grow only in dry corners of southern Arabia, Socotra and the Horn of Africa. Getting them to the Mediterranean took camels, ships and many middlemen.
evidence.now: A shop near Campo Santo Stefano sells dozens of resins under glass. Read the labels: myrrh from Yemen, frankincense and dragon's blood from Socotra.
evidence.gone: The caravans, the ports where the resin changed hands, and the prices that once made it worth more than most metals.
optic: Read the small white labels. Which places are named?
Why might a shop in Venice still sell resin from Socotra today?

evidence.title: A bowl of frankincense
evidence.then: Frankincense is dried sap. Workers cut the bark of the Boswellia tree, and the milky resin hardens into pale lumps.
evidence.now: Loose frankincense in a wooden bowl, sold by weight.
evidence.gone: We can't tell from the photo where these grains were harvested, or how many hands they passed through.
optic: Describe the colour and size of the grains.
What would you need to know to trace these grains back to a tree?

evidence.title: One large piece of resin
evidence.then: Resins were sold by size and quality. The best pieces were large, clear and pale.
evidence.now: A single lump of golden resin held up for the camera. The hand gives you the scale.
evidence.gone: Which resin this is. The photo alone can't tell us.
optic: Use the hand to estimate the size of the piece.
What question would you ask the shopkeeper?

evidence.title: An incense burner from Damascus
evidence.site: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
evidence.then: Made in Damascus under the Mamluks, late 1200s to early 1300s. Brass inlaid with silver and gold. Smoke from frankincense would have drifted out through the pierced dome.
evidence.now: It sits in a glass case in New York, more than 9,000 km from where it was used. Met accession number 17.190.1716.
evidence.gone: The smell. The room it was used in. The people who lit it.
optic: Find the Arabic writing and the seated figure on the burner.
Why is evidence of the spice trade so often found far from where it happened?

evidence.title: The museum's label
evidence.site: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
evidence.then: The label is a secondary source: a museum's summary of what experts know about the object.
evidence.now: It gives a place (Damascus), a period (Mamluk, 1250–1517), materials, and how the museum got it (a 1917 gift).
evidence.gone: The label doesn't say how the burner travelled from Syria to a New York collector.
optic: List three facts the label gives.
What does the label leave out?

evidence.title: A painting of a Cairo mosque
evidence.site: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
evidence.then: Jean-Léon Gérôme, a French painter, painted worshippers in an old Cairo mosque in 1871. It is a European artist's view of the Islamic world, not a photograph.
evidence.now: Hanging in New York.
evidence.gone: The painter's point of view hides as much as it shows. Ask what he chose to include.
optic: Who made this, and for whom?
What makes a painting different from a photograph as evidence?

mismatch.actual: The photo's GPS places it at the Met in New York, and the painting shows a mosque in Cairo.

evidence.title: Inside the Mezquita of Córdoba
evidence.then: Begun under Abd al-Rahman I in the 780s, the great mosque grew as Córdoba became one of the richest cities in Europe, linked to trade across the Islamic world.
evidence.now: The arches and domes still stand. Since 1236 the building has been a cathedral.
evidence.gone: The markets, gardens and scholars of Muslim Córdoba. You have to imagine them.
optic: Describe the patterns in the arches.
What can a building tell you about a city's wealth and connections?

evidence.title: Synagogue of Córdoba
evidence.then: Built around 1315, after Christian kings had taken the city. Its plaster uses the same style as Islamic buildings nearby.
evidence.now: One of very few medieval synagogues left in Spain.
evidence.gone: The Jewish community that prayed here. Jews were expelled from Spain in 1492.
optic: The style looks like a mosque's. What does that suggest about the people who built it?

evidence.title: Hebrew letters in the plaster
evidence.then: Hebrew inscriptions run through Islamic-style plasterwork: mixture you can see.
evidence.now: The inscriptions survive; the women's gallery opening is above.
evidence.gone: Most of the building's original colour and furnishings.
optic: Find the Hebrew writing. Where is it placed?
What does this mixing of styles tell you?

evidence.title: Horses carved in stone
evidence.then: Vijayanagara's kings bought warhorses shipped from Arabia and Persia, paid for in part with the wealth of India's spice coasts. Niccolò de' Conti visited the city in the 1400s.
evidence.now: Friezes of horses and their handlers line the temple bases.
evidence.gone: The horse traders and the market. Vijayanagara was sacked in 1565.
optic: Look at the handlers. Do they look local or foreign? How can you tell?
Why would a kingdom carve horses onto a temple?

evidence.title: More horses at Hampi
evidence.then: Horses didn't breed well in south India's climate, so they had to be imported again and again.
evidence.now: A second frieze: a procession of horses and a man leading them.
evidence.gone: Written records of the trade are scattered. The stone is one of the clearest traces.
optic: Compare this frieze with the first one. What repeats?

evidence.title: Virupaksha temple, Hampi
evidence.then: The heart of a capital that foreign visitors compared to Rome.
evidence.now: The temple is still used for worship. Most of the city around it is ruins.
evidence.gone: The bazaar that ran in front of the temple, where visitors described piles of goods and jewels.
optic: What survives here, and what doesn't?

evidence.title: Fondaco dei Tedeschi
evidence.then: A fondaco (from the Arabic funduq) was a walled warehouse where foreign merchants had to live, store goods and pay taxes. German merchants came here to buy spices and carry them north.
evidence.now: The building, rebuilt after a fire in 1505, still stands on the Grand Canal. It has been a post office and a shopping centre.
evidence.gone: The merchants, the sacks of pepper, the customs officers.
optic: Look at the barred ground-floor windows. Why might a warehouse need them?
The word fondaco came from Arabic. What does that tell you?

evidence.title: Model of a Venetian galley
evidence.then: Galleys like this sailed in the muda, the convoy that left Venice each year to buy spices in Alexandria and Beirut.
evidence.now: A model in a museum. No real merchant galley survives.
evidence.gone: Every real galley. Wooden ships rot, sink or are broken up.
optic: Count the oars on one side. What does that tell you about the crew?

evidence.title: The Doge's golden barge
evidence.then: The Bucintoro was not a trading ship. The Doge used it once a year to 'marry the sea', showing that Venice's wealth came from the water.
evidence.now: A model. The last real Bucintoro was destroyed in 1798 after Napoleon took Venice.
evidence.gone: The ship itself.
optic: Compare it with the galley. Which was built for work, and which for show?

evidence.title: The Grand Canal from the Rialto
evidence.then: Rialto was Venice's market, where spices brought by the muda were sold to merchants from all over Europe.
evidence.now: Palaces built with trade money line the canal. Today the boats carry tourists.
evidence.gone: The spice stalls and the noise of bargaining in many languages.
optic: Which buildings look oldest? What clues tell you they were built by rich families?

evidence.title: Palaces at sunset
evidence.then: A city built on islands, with no fields to farm. Its wealth came from trade.
evidence.now: The same view, with gondolas.
evidence.gone: Almost every sign of where the money came from.
optic: Nothing in this photo shows spice. How could you prove spice paid for it?

evidence.title: The Fra Mauro map
evidence.then: Made around 1450 by Fra Mauro, a monk on the island of Murano, from travellers' reports including Niccolò de' Conti's. It shows Africa as a continent you could sail around. South is at the top.
evidence.now: It hangs in the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice.
evidence.gone: A copy made for the King of Portugal is lost. The map that may have encouraged Portugal's voyages no longer exists.
optic: SCRAP: Find the Mediterranean. Then find the Indian Ocean.
Use the flip button. Why might Fra Mauro put south at the top?

evidence.title: A book of secrets
evidence.site: Venice, at or near Palazzo Mocenigo (perfume museum)
evidence.then: Books of 'secrets' gave recipes for medicines, perfumes and dyes, many using spices. This one, by 'Alessio Piemontese', was a best-seller for two centuries.
evidence.now: An old edition open in a case, beside jars once used for ingredients.
evidence.gone: Whether the recipes worked.
optic: The jars have labels. What were they for?

mismatch.actual: The photo's GPS places it in Venice, near Palazzo Mocenigo, about 30 km from Padua.

evidence.title: Apothecary bottles at Padua
evidence.then: Padua's botanical garden, founded in 1545, is the oldest university garden still in its original place. Students learned to identify medicinal plants, many of them spices.
evidence.now: Old pharmacy bottles on display.
evidence.gone: There was no line between a spice shop and a pharmacy. That line came later.
optic: Read any label you can. Is it a food, a medicine, or both?

evidence.title: A spice shop in Thessaloniki
evidence.then: Thessaloniki was an Ottoman port where many Sephardic Jews settled after 1492.
evidence.now: Herbs, teas and spices sold loose by weight, in Greek.
evidence.gone: Nothing here tells you which ingredients travelled furthest. That's the point: spices are now ordinary.
optic: Which of these might have come from another continent?

months.text: Northeast monsoon. Ships sail from India west to Arabia and Africa.
Northeast monsoon. Pepper ships head for Aden and the Red Sea.
The northeast winds weaken. Last westbound sailings.
Changing winds. Cargo moves up the Red Sea and overland to Cairo.
Changing winds. Ports fill with ships waiting for the turn.
Southwest monsoon. Strong winds blow from Africa toward India. Storms close many Indian ports.
Southwest monsoon at full strength. Few ships risk the open sea.
Southwest monsoon. Ships from the Red Sea set out for India. In Venice, galleys are fitted out for the muda.
Late southwest monsoon. Ships reach the Malabar coast. The Venetian convoy sails for Alexandria.
Changing winds. Spices from India reach Alexandria, where Venetian merchants are waiting to buy.
Northeast monsoon begins. Loaded galleys head home across the Mediterranean.
Northeast monsoon. The convoy arrives in Venice, in time for buyers from northern Europe.
